definition: Abscond means to sneak away secretly, often taking something along.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word abscond. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know abscond should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The apprentice absconded before dawn with the master glassblower's pattern book, leaving his tools and half a year's wages behind.
Depart is perfectly neutral — a train departs on schedule; depart stops far short of abscond, which slips away in secret with something it should not have.
Vanish goes further than abscond: the absconder is somewhere down the road with the cash box and a guilty conscience, while a person who vanishes leaves no trail at all.

To flee is to run from danger or pursuit — a fire, a flood, the law — and it can be done openly, in full panic, before a hundred witnesses. Abscond adds what flee leaves out: secrecy, planning, and usually something carried off that the absconder should not have.

Decamp means to pack up and clear out suddenly — literally to strike camp — and it can be perfectly innocent: an army decamps at dawn, a weary houseguest decamps. Abscond is never innocent: whoever absconds slips away in secret, usually with money or goods, dodging a debt or an arrest.

Abscond means to sneak away secretly, often taking something along.

For six seasons the touring company trusted its advance agent to carry the box-office takings between towns; in Dover he absconded with the strongbox, having quietly bought a steamer passage under another name.

Abscond is more exact than 'run away' or 'flee' because it adds secrecy and usually something carried off — a person absconds quietly, often with money or goods not their own, and typically to dodge arrest or a debt.
Abscond is the auditor's and the reporter's verb — treasurers abscond with funds, clerks abscond with the till.
In casual talk 'ran off with' does the same work; choose abscond when you want the guilty stealth on the record, and note how naturally it pairs with 'with.'

In the spring of 1872 the town of Fairview voted its entire road fund to a contractor who promised an iron bridge by autumn.
He sank two stone piers, staged one noisy ceremony, and then absconded in the night with the remaining money, leaving a half-built crossing and a ledger of unpaid suppliers.
For weeks the council insisted he had merely gone east to inspect girders.
But his rooms had been emptied quietly, his accounts closed days before, and the stagecoach office had no record of any ticket in his name.
The town finished the bridge itself years later, and wrote into its charter a rule born of the affair: no public money would ever again be paid out faster than the work rose.
